resolved_by: Congress enacted the Abolish Trafficking Reauthorization Act (ATRA), which amended 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a) to add attempt-to-benefit civil liability, labeled a 'technical and clarifying' update. The majority held it applies to pending cases as a clarification, not a retroactive change.
issue: Does civil liability under the TVPRA's civil remedy, 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), extend to a defendant who attempted to benefit from a trafficking violation, where the statute's 'knowingly benefits' clause omits the word 'attempt'?

sides.position: Civil liability extends to one who attempts to benefit from a TVPRA violation, because the omission of 'attempt' in the civil provision was an oversight (position attributed to two unnamed circuits by the dissent).
Section 1595(a) does not reach one who merely attempts to benefit from a TVPRA violation; the text is unambiguous and 'attempt' cannot be read into the 'knowingly benefits' clause.
cases: Ratha v. Rubicon Resources, LLC, 35 F.4th 1171 (9th Cir. 2022)
Keo Ratha v. Rubicon Resources, LLC, 111 F.4th 946 (9th Cir. 2024)

quote: Two other circuits implicitly concluded that this omission was an oversight, ruling that an attempt to benefit from human trafficking creates civil liability. This court disagreed in Ratha I, creating a circuit split.
cite: Keo Ratha v. Rubicon Resources, LLC, 111 F.4th 946 (9th Cir. 2024)
